subject: Communication
title: Hofstede's Cultural Dimensions
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Hofstede's Cultural Dimensions.

hook.text: Geert Hofstede surveyed 116,000 IBM employees across 72 countries. He found that culture could be measured on six axes.

buildup.text: His six dimensions: Power Distance, Individualism, Masculinity, Uncertainty Avoidance, Long-Term Orientation, and Indulgence.

discovery.text: Each dimension is a spectrum. Every country scores differently, creating a unique cultural fingerprint.

twist.text: Hofstede's model is powerful but imperfect — it treats nations as uniform and ignores subcultures, generations, and individuals.

climax.text: Despite its limits, the framework gave global businesses their first systematic language for discussing cultural differences.

punchline.text: Culture can't be measured perfectly. But it can be mapped usefully.

quiz.question: How many cultural dimensions did Hofstede identify?

details.summary: Geert Hofstede identified six dimensions that differentiate national cultures: power distance, individualism, masculinity, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation, and indulgence. These measurable dimensions help predict communication patterns across 70-plus countries.
details.whyItMatters: Hofstede's framework gives you a practical map for anticipating communication differences before you encounter them, reducing surprise and friction.
takeaways: Six dimensions map cultural differences across countries
Power distance and individualism are the most impactful for communication
The framework helps predict, not stereotype

faq.question: What are the main criticisms of Hofstede's model?
faq.answer: Critics note it was based on IBM employees in the 1970s, equates culture with nationality, and oversimplifies complex societies. It cannot account for subcultures, generational shifts, or individual variation. It is best used as a starting framework, not a definitive guide.

faq.question: How should you use cultural dimensions in practice?
faq.answer: Use them to form hypotheses, not conclusions. If a country scores high on power distance, expect that hierarchy may matter more, but verify with observation. Combine the framework with individual relationship building. The map is not the territory.
